hint1: Back when mammoths still roamed, my ancestors grazed steppe stretching from the Carpathians clear across to Beringia—my commute has shrunk a bit since then.
hint2: Nowadays my particular herd sticks to one corner of the map, long gone from places like Ukraine, Moldova, and China.
hint3: I'm the western Mongolia-only branch of a steppe grazer—found nowhere else on the planet, not even elsewhere in Mongolia.
funFacts: During the Pleistocene, this species' range stretched incredibly far, from the British Isles all the way to Beringia. Today one subspecies survives only in a sliver of western Mongolia, having vanished entirely from Romania, Ukraine, Moldova, China, and the rest of Mongolia.

hint1: I strut through the steamy jungles of Borneo, Sumatra, and the Malay Peninsula like I own the place—because, well, I kind of do.
hint2: My feathers are so over-the-top for courtship that I practically invented the dance floor before anyone else thought of it.
hint3: I'm a giant, flamboyant pheasant often mixed up with a crested cousin who isn't nearly as extra as me.
funFacts: Despite being famous for its jaw-dropping courtship display, this pheasant is often confused with the crested argus—even though the two belong to entirely different genera.

hint1: I'm one of the newest large mammals science has met—yet I've been hiding in plain sight for ages.
hint2: My homeland is a rugged mountain range straddling the border of two Southeast Asian countries.
hint3: Scientists first proved I existed after finding my remains in a Vietnamese national park in the early 1990s.
funFacts: This forest bovid was unknown to science until 1993, when a joint survey team found its remains in Vũ Quang National Park. Every attempt to keep one in captivity has ended within weeks or months, making it one of the most elusive large mammals on Earth.

hint1: Count my headgear before you count your guesses — I don't just have the usual two.
hint2: I'm a shy, small Indian grass-nibbler, barely knee-high on you, in a goldenrod coat.
hint3: My forehead sprouts a second, stubby pair of horns in front of my main set — a bovid oddity if ever there was one.
funFacts: This is the only antelope in the world with four horns instead of two, and the front pair can be so tiny they're just fur-covered nubs rather than true horns. The rear horns are always the longer of the two sets, reaching up to about 12 cm.

hint1: I'm a homebody of flooded forests, sticking close to water in the far western Amazon where Brazil meets Peru.
hint2: My tail is embarrassingly short for a monkey, but I make up for it with a seriously luxurious coat.
hint3: My head has zero hair and my face goes shockingly crimson — like I've been caught blushing forever.
funFacts: Unlike most New World monkeys, which use long prehensile tails for climbing, this species gets by with a stubby one. It lives only in wooded, waterlogged várzea habitats of the western Amazon, a surprisingly narrow home range for such a memorable-looking primate.

hint2: You'll find me hanging out in swampy backwaters, riverside forests, and mangroves along two great South American river systems.
hint3: I'm the one and only living species in my genus, family, and order, native to the Amazon and Orinoco basins.
funFacts: This bird is so taxonomically unique that it stands alone as the sole living member of its entire order, family, and genus. Scientists still debate exactly where it fits on the bird family tree.

hint1: I'm so oddly specific that taxonomists just shrugged and built me a whole family of my own, no roommates included.
hint2: Picture red stilts for legs, a bill that curves downward like it's perpetually unimpressed, and a black mask across my face.
hint3: Grey body, white belly, black face and breast band, red legs, and a long down-curved bill - I pick my way over shingle riverbanks high in the mountains of central Asia and the Himalayas.
funFacts: Despite looking like a distant cousin of the waders, this bird is considered distinctive enough to have an entire family, Ibidorhynchidae, all to itself. It makes its home on stony river shingle across the high plateaux of central Asia and the Himalayas, a stark, rocky habitat that suits its camouflage-colored plumage perfectly.

hint1: I split my year between two very different shores: a chilly northern sea and the tropical hush of Southeast Asia.

funFacts: This tiny wader's unique spatulate beak helps it sift through mud for food, and by 2000 its entire breeding population was estimated at just 350–500 individuals—making it one of the rarest birds on the planet.
